topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: What does the programmer’s model omit?
options: The CPU registers and their names
Individual transistors and internal bus construction
The specified effects of register reads
explanations: Registers are visible software state, so they belong in the model.
Implementation details such as individual transistors and bus-matrix construction; it retains registers, addresses and the specified effects of accesses.
Those effects are exactly what software needs the model to describe.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: List the visible state and hidden implementation in a programmer’s model.
options: Transistors are visible; stacks and modes are hidden
Pipeline stages are visible; peripheral registers are hidden
Registers, addresses and exceptions are visible; pipeline construction is hidden
explanations: Code uses stacks and execution modes, not individual transistors.
Software names peripheral registers, while the pipeline implementation is normally hidden.
Visible: CPU registers, memory, peripheral registers, modes/stacks and exceptions. Hidden: individual transistors, pipeline construction and bus matrix internals.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: Name all five parts of this Cortex-M programmer’s model.
options: Registers, caches, transistors, compiler and linker
Flash, SRAM, heap, stack and local variables
Registers, one address map, peripherals, modes/stacks and exceptions
explanations: Compiler/linker are tools; caches/transistors do not replace the visible mode and exception rules.
These are memory categories, not all five parts of the machine model.
Registers; unified memory map; memory-mapped peripheral state; Thread/Handler modes with MSP/PSP; vectored exception handling.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: How does the CPU reach state outside its own registers?
options: Only through calls into an operating system
Loads and stores to addresses in the common map
Dedicated IN/OUT instructions for every device
explanations: Bare-metal code can access mapped hardware directly without an OS.
By address using loads/stores; this chip has no separate I/O port instruction space.
Cortex-M does not use a separate I/O instruction space.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: Give three differences between a device register and a RAM variable.
options: Hardware can change it, a read can consume data, and a write can drive a pin
It always stores bytes exactly like SRAM, but at a higher address
Only software changes it and reads have no effects
explanations: Register values can change asynchronously; reads can acknowledge/consume events; writes can affect physical pins or start operations.
The address selects a device with documented effects, not ordinary storage.
Peripheral hardware also changes state and some reads acknowledge events.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: Describe control, status and data register roles and who accesses them.
options: Software configures control, checks status and transfers data; hardware updates status
Software writes status to invent received data; hardware reads control as payload
Control, status and data are three names for interchangeable registers
explanations: Software writes control settings, reads hardware status, and reads/writes payload data as appropriate. Hardware updates status and received data.
Status reports actual device state; control selects behavior, not payload.
Their access rules and meanings differ; interchanging them can change hardware accidentally.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: Which manual answers NVIC priority versus USART pin routing?
options: ARM for NVIC priority; ST for USART pin routing
The board schematic for NVIC priority; ARM for USART alternate functions
ST for both because ST manufactures the whole chip
explanations: ARM’s core guide explains NVIC. ST’s reference manual/datasheet explains vendor registers and alternate-function pin choices.
A schematic describes wiring; ARM does not define this vendor pin multiplexer.
NVIC behavior belongs to the ARM core architecture; ST documents vendor pin routing.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: A peripheral ignores configuration and reads zero. What is the first suspect?
options: The RCC clock gate is disabled
The register should be declared const instead of volatile
The peripheral needs a RAM allocation first
explanations: Its RCC clock gate. Without a clock the device can ignore stores and return zero.
const does not power or clock hardware and would prevent configuration writes.
A mapped device exists independently of the program heap.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: Name two causes of garbled or missing serial output from this model.
options: Too many general-purpose CPU registers or an odd Thumb target
Wrong UART-clock divisor or wrong pin alternate function
A missing printf newline or little-endian RAM by itself
explanations: Register count does not set baud; the odd target is the valid Thumb marker.
A divisor computed from the wrong UART clock produces wrong baud; incorrect pin mux/alternate function prevents correct signal routing.
Neither explains a wrong bit rate or disconnected TX route.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: Why can casting a byte buffer to a word pointer HardFault on M0+? Would M3 necessarily fail?
options: Any byte buffer is unreadable by M3 because it is an 8-bit object
Casting automatically aligns the address on both cores
The cast may produce an unaligned word access; M3 ordinary loads may support it
explanations: Byte storage is readable; the issue is alignment and access instructions, not the label of the object.
A cast changes the pointer type, not where the buffer starts.
The buffer may not be naturally 4-byte aligned. M0+ disallows the unaligned word access; M3 ordinary loads may support it with extra cost.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: Which three implementation effects must firmware account for?
options: Pipeline/PC effects, bus clock gates and flash wait-state ordering
Only the C type sizes; hardware timing is always hidden
Only cache replacement and virtual page faults
explanations: Pipeline/branch and PC behavior; different bus clock gates; flash wait states ordered before frequency increases.
Branches, clocks and flash timing have visible effects firmware must handle.
This small MCU uses wait states and has no desktop MMU/page-fault model.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: How does USART2 reach its handler without a registration call?
options: The linker calls USART2_IRQHandler every time a byte arrives
USART2 searches RAM for a matching function name
Hardware uses vector entry 44, selected by IRQ 28
explanations: The linker builds addresses; hardware selects the handler at runtime.
Hardware follows a vector address, not source-language names.
IRQ 28 selects vector 16+28=44, whose stored function address is loaded by hardware.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: Compare port-mapped and memory-mapped I/O and classify AVR and Cortex-M.
options: Memory-mapped I/O means every peripheral register is SRAM
AVR has dedicated I/O operations; Cortex-M uses ordinary mapped loads/stores
Both need x86 IN/OUT for every GPIO access
explanations: Mapped devices share address syntax with RAM but keep device-specific behavior.
Port mapping provides a separate I/O space and dedicated instructions, as in AVR IN/OUT. Cortex-M maps devices into the ordinary address space.
Cortex-M has mapped device registers, not x86 port instructions.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: Why did AVR need PROGMEM and LPM for flash constants?
options: PROGMEM makes volatile reads atomic
LPM enables a peripheral clock before reading flash
AVR flash is in a separate program-memory space
explanations: PROGMEM concerns placement/access to flash, not concurrency.
LPM is a program-memory load, not an RCC clock command.
Its Harvard code/data spaces require separate program-memory access. The unified Cortex-M map reads flash constants through ordinary pointers.

topicTitle: The five parts of the machine
question: What provides desktop virtual-memory protection, and what can a bad pointer do here?
options: The MCU MMU redirects every bad pointer to private task RAM
An MPU creates virtual addresses just like an MMU
A desktop MMU maps/protects virtual memory; this MCU pointer can reach RAM or devices
explanations: This chip lacks an MMU and separate task virtual maps.
An MPU checks permissions on real addresses; it does not perform virtual translation.

A desktop MMU translates/enforces virtual memory. This chip lacks it; a bad pointer can corrupt shared real RAM, reach a device, or fault at an unmapped address. Optional MPUs provide permissions without virtual maps.

question: Where is the zero flag, and how is PRIMASK accessed?
options: Z is APSR bit 30; MRS/MSR access PRIMASK
Z is APSR bit 30; LDR at a peripheral address reads PRIMASK
Z is stored in GPIO status; a RAM pointer accesses PRIMASK
explanations: Z is xPSR/APSR bit 30. PRIMASK is a special core register accessed by MRS/MSR or CMSIS intrinsics, not a memory pointer.
Knowing the flag location does not make PRIMASK memory-mapped; it needs special-register access.
Z and PRIMASK are CPU state, not GPIO or normal memory registers.

question: What bytes represent 0x12345678 in STM32 RAM?
options: 87 65 43 21, in increasing addresses
78 56 34 12, in increasing addresses
12 34 56 78, in increasing addresses
explanations: Endianness rearranges whole bytes; it does not reverse bits or hexadecimal digits inside each byte.
78 56 34 12 at successive addresses; the least significant byte comes first.
That is big-endian ordering; STM32 puts the least significant byte first.

topicTitle: Peripheral roles and the correct manual
question: Why can reading a register be dangerous?
options: Only writes can ever change a device
A read may clear an event or consume a byte
A read always overwrites every register in the peripheral
explanations: Read side effects are part of many peripheral access rules.
A read can acknowledge an event or remove a received byte. Treating it like a repeatable RAM read can change device state accidentally.
Read effects are register-specific; they do not universally reset a whole block.

question: USART2 is IRQ 28. Which vector and IPSR value apply?
options: Vector 44 and IPSR 44 (0x2C)
Vector 44 but IPSR remains zero
Vector 28 and IPSR 28
explanations: 16+28=44. Vector entry 44 holds its target and IPSR records exception 44 while the handler executes.
IPSR is zero in Thread mode; an executing handler reports its exception identity.
External IRQ numbers start after 16 core vector entries; both use exception number 44 here.

topicTitle: Clock gates, pin ownership and implementation costs
question: A configured peripheral reads zero. What should you check first?
options: Check the RCC clock gate first
Change the pin pull-up first, because it powers the peripheral
Install a new handler before checking the clock
explanations: Its RCC clock gate, then the addressed block and pin mux. Configuration writes cannot take effect while its clock is disabled.
A pull resistor biases a pin; it does not provide the device clock.
Handler installation cannot make unclocked configuration registers work.

topicTitle: Reading Thumb code and recognizing its limits
question: Can a Cortex-M switch to A32 to get divide instructions?
options: No; M0+ uses software division and M3/M4 have Thumb divide instructions
Yes; clearing the Thumb bit enables A32 divide
No Cortex-M supports division even through software
explanations: No Cortex-M has A32 state. M0+ division uses a library; M3/M4 provide Thumb-2 divide instructions.
Cortex-M has no A32 execution state; clearing the tag gives an invalid target.
Software can implement division; larger Cortex-M cores also have hardware Thumb division.

topicTitle: Loads, arithmetic, bit fields and conditions
question: Why does unsigned 0xFFFFFFFF compare differently from signed -1?
options: CMP knows the C type and chooses the branch automatically
A signed cast changes every bit in the register
The same bits mean 4294967295 unsigned but −1 signed, with different branch tests
explanations: CMP creates flags; the compiler selects signed or unsigned branch conditions.
Interpretation changes without changing that bit pattern.
The bit pattern is identical, but unsigned comparison treats it as 4294967295 and uses carry-based branches; signed comparison treats it as negative and uses N/V.

topicTitle: Calls, the ABI and tagged return addresses
question: LR reads 0x0800028F. Where does an ordinary return resume?
options: 0x0800028A, re-executing the call
0x0800028F, executing an instruction at the odd byte
0x0800028E, after removing the Thumb tag
explanations: LR points after BL, not to the calling instruction itself.
Bit 0 marks Thumb state; the actual instruction starts at the aligned address.
0x0800028E: clear the Thumb tag, retaining the address of the instruction immediately after the call.

question: Can a narrow LDR reach offset 128?
options: No; all narrow loads can reach only 31 bytes
Yes; its immediate is an unscaled 8-bit byte offset
No; narrow base-relative LDR reaches 124 bytes
explanations: LDRB reaches 31 bytes; word LDR scales its offset and reaches 124.
This narrow form uses five bits scaled by four, not an eight-bit byte offset.
No. Its maximum is 31×4=124 bytes; the compiler must adjust a base or use an available wider architecture encoding.

question: Why is there no BL to put in the optimized loop?
options: All C function calls use B instead of BL on M0+
put was inlined into the two send blocks
The linker deleted transmission as unused
explanations: BL is supported; this missing call results from inlining, not the ISA.
The helper was inlined: its polling and store instructions appear directly in two send blocks.
The send instructions remain in the loop; only the separate helper call disappears.

question: How many mnemonics covered roughly 80% of the cited image?
options: Thirteen entries prove those instructions consume 79.6% of execution time
Thirteen grouped entries, totaling 79.6% of this static image
All 51 mnemonics appear equally often
explanations: Static counts do not measure how often loops run at runtime.
Thirteen, counting PUSH/POP together in the frequency table; their cumulative share was79.6% in the -Os spike image.
The listed proportions are strongly unequal; a small group dominates this image.

question: Why does setting an ODR bit involve three core operations?
options: Each C assignment is one indivisible machine instruction
Load ODR, change the register value, store it back
ORRS changes ODR directly through its address operand
explanations: C expressions can compile to several instructions and can be interrupted between them.
Load current word, modify a register operand, then store the word. A load–store ALU cannot update a memory bit directly; BSRR avoids the read by accepting a command.
ORRS operates on CPU registers; a separate store commits device state.

question: Which C mask operation corresponds to BICS?
options: x |= mask
x ^= mask
x &= ~mask
explanations: OR inserts selected ones; BICS removes selected bits.
XOR toggles selected bits; BICS clears them regardless of their previous state.
x &= ~mask: preserve only bits not selected in the mask.

question: Why does the sample contain more shifts than subtraction?
options: Shifts occur only in the division helper
M0+ implements every subtraction as a shift
Pin-field setup frequently builds shifted masks
explanations: GPIO field placement also needs shifts, independently of division.
SUBS exists; the measured shift count reflects the application fields.
GPIO/peripheral field setup repeatedly computes shifted masks and values, making LSLS common.

question: CMP discards its subtraction result. What useful state remains?
options: The subtraction result replaces the first operand
N, Z, C and V flags remain for branch decisions
Only the Z flag can change
explanations: CMP updates flags without retaining the arithmetic result in that operand.
The N/Z/C/V flags encode equality, sign, unsigned carry/no-borrow and signed overflow for later branches.
CMP supplies sign, carry/no-borrow and overflow flags as well as equality.

question: How do BLT and BCC differ?
options: BLT uses signed N/V; BCC uses unsigned carry
BLT uses carry; BCC compares N and V
They are interchangeable spellings of less-than
explanations: BLT tests signed less-than using N/V; BCC tests unsigned lower-than using carry. Interchanging them misinterprets high-bit-set values.
This swaps their meanings and gives incorrect results for negative bit patterns.
High-bit-set values distinguish signed and unsigned comparisons.

question: What extra action does POP {r4,pc} perform versus restoring LR?
options: It restores registers and branches to the saved target through PC
It restores PC as data but execution continues to the next instruction
It creates a fresh return address in LR
explanations: It loads the saved target directly into PC, combining register restoration with the function return.
Writing PC changes control flow; POP PC performs the return.
POP consumes saved stack values; BL creates a link-register return target.

question: Identify the addressing modes for s->field and buf[i].
options: s->field uses a fixed base offset; buf[i] can use a runtime register offset
Both require a literal pool for every element
s->field uses the current PC; buf[i] always uses SP
explanations: A struct member uses a fixed immediate offset from its base; a byte-array element can use a register offset for the runtime index.
A literal pool loads constants; ordinary member/array access uses an address calculation.
Their bases come from the relevant pointers, not necessarily PC or SP.

question: How does M0+ perform division, and what evidence appears in a map?
options: A software helper such as __aeabi_uidiv; the map can include _udivsi3.o
The compiler evaluates every division at build time
SDIV runs directly on the M0+ integer ALU
explanations: It calls a software routine such as __aeabi_uidiv. A map can show libgcc _udivsi3.o pulled into the image.
Only constant cases can be folded; runtime operands need runtime division.
M0+ has no hardware divide instruction.

question: What is A32, and when can this Cortex-M enter it?
options: Handler mode automatically switches Cortex-M to A32
A32 means any Thumb instruction occupying 32 bits
A32 is ARM’s 32-bit instruction state; this Cortex-M never enters it
explanations: Exceptions remain in Thumb execution on Cortex-M.
Encoding width and execution state are different; wide Thumb is still Thumb.
A32 is ARM’s32-bit instruction state. Cortex-M never enters it; its decoder supports Thumb only.

question: Name three operations a Cortex-M4 can encode directly that M0+ needs multiple instructions or a helper for.
options: M4 adds only floating-point and no extra integer forms
Hardware divide, a large load offset and MOVW/MOVT constant construction
Every M4 instruction is supported on M0+ but takes more cycles
explanations: Full Thumb-2 adds integer operations and addressing; floating-point depends on the variant.
Hardware division; a large base-relative load such asoffset2000; building a 32-bit constant with MOVW/MOVT without a literal pool. The M4 also supports wider addressing forms.
M0+ cannot decode the full M4 instruction set.

question: The vector is 0x08000275 but code starts0x08000274. Explain the one-bit difference.
options: Bit 0 tags Thumb; instructions start at the even address
The odd value means the linker created an unaligned instruction
The first byte at 0x08000274 is padding that execution skips
explanations: Bit0 tags Thumb state. It does not add a byte to the instruction address; clearing it makes an invalid target state on Cortex-M.
Instruction placement remains aligned; function target encoding carries the tag.
The odd target contains a state tag, not a one-byte code offset.

question: Given LR0x0800028F, what runs after return and what could an even target imply?
options: Resume at the vector-table base; LR always stores a vector index
Resume at 0x0800028E; an even computed target can mean a missing Thumb tag
Resume at 0x0800028F; even targets are always safer
explanations: An ordinary LR is a return target, not an index; exceptions use a distinct EXC_RETURN encoding.
Return resumes0x0800028E. A computed even function target/LR can indicate a missing Thumb tag and cause a fault.
Thumb targets need the state tag while the instruction address is even.

question: Classify x86, Cortex-M and AVR as register–memory or load–store.
options: All three do arithmetic directly on arbitrary memory operands
x86 is register–memory; Cortex-M and AVR are load–store, with selected AVR I/O exceptions
Cortex-M is a stack machine and x86 is load–store
explanations: Cortex-M ALU arithmetic uses registers; AVR has only selected I/O exceptions.
x86 is register–memory; Cortex-M and AVR are load–store, with AVR’s selected SBI I/O bit operations as an exception.
Cortex-M uses register operands; x86 supports memory operands in arithmetic.

question: How does RISC-V implement a signed comparison branch without APSR, and what do ARM flags buy?
options: RISC-V blt compares operands directly; ARM CMP produces reusable flags
ARM CMP branches immediately and cannot feed later tests
RISC-V blt first writes an ARM APSR register
explanations: RISC-V can use blt a 0,a 1,L directly. ARM CMP sets reusable flags that can feed several branches, improving encoding density at the cost of hidden dependencies.
CMP sets flags; subsequent branches can reuse them until another instruction changes them.
RISC-V does not depend on ARM’s APSR flag state.

question: Contrast stack return addresses with link registers. Why save LR in a non-leaf function?
options: Every ARM BL automatically pushes the old LR to memory
BL overwrites LR, so a function making another call must save its own return target
Leaf functions must always save LR, while nested callers never do
explanations: BL writes LR without automatically stacking its previous value.
A stack-call instruction stores each return in memory. BL puts it in LR, so a laterBL overwrites it; savingLR first preserves the caller’s return.
A leaf can keep its return in LR; nested calls overwrite it and require preservation.

question: Why can a narrow instruction not contain0x40021000, and how do architectures solve that?
options: A 16-bit instruction stores a full 32-bit address after its opcode
Too few immediate bits; Thumb uses a literal pool, RISC-V LUI/ADDI, x86 a longer encoding
Every architecture places all peripheral addresses in a dedicated CPU register
explanations: Its total width cannot hold 32 address bits plus opcode/operands.
Opcode/register bits leave too little immediate space. Thumb loads a literal near code; RISC-V builds it withLUI/ADDI; variable-length x86 embeds a larger immediate.
Architectures encode or construct constants differently; there is no universal dedicated address register.

question: A header declares SystemCoreClock but linking fails. What is missing?
options: Another extern declaration in the same header
A linked object must define storage for SystemCoreClock
A larger heap allocation at runtime
explanations: Repeating declarations does not allocate storage or provide a definition.
A storage definition in an object included in the link. A declaration lets a file compile; it does not allocate the variable.
The linker needs a symbol definition before runtime begins.

question: Why does a nonzero initialized global cost both flash and RAM?
options: Flash preserves the initial value; SRAM holds the writable runtime copy
The global stays only in Flash because it has an initial value
Flash and SRAM mirror each write automatically
explanations: Its starting value must survive power loss in flash while its runtime value must remain writable in RAM; startup copies between them.
A writable global needs SRAM during execution despite its persistent initial image.
Startup copies initial bytes once; ordinary SRAM writes do not update Flash.

question: What does Intel HEX type04 with data0800 establish?
options: It writes data value 0x0800 into SRAM
It sets the program entry point to 0x00000800
Upper address bits become 0x0800, so offset zero targets 0x08000000
explanations: Type 04 sets the address context for later data records; it is not a SRAM data write.
An extended linear address record sets high address bits, not the reset target.
The upper16 address bits become0x0800; an offset 0000 data record therefore targets0x08000000.

question: Name the build’s five stages and the one made explicit in embedded work.
options: Preprocess, compile, assemble, link, locate; preprocess fixes all symbol addresses
Compile, execute, debug, print, reset; reset assigns addresses
Preprocess, compile, assemble, link, locate; locate fixes physical placement
explanations: Preprocessing expands text; final addresses depend on linked sections and placement.
Execution and debugging occur after building; physical placement belongs to the linker script.
Preprocess,compile,assemble,link,locate. Locate binds sections/symbols to the chip’s physical addresses through the linker script.

question: Does .data occupy flash or RAM?
options: Only Flash; startup uses it directly as writable storage
Both: Flash load image and writable SRAM run location
Only SRAM because writable data cannot have a Flash copy
explanations: Ordinary runtime writes cannot treat Flash as SRAM; startup creates the writable copy.
Both: flash stores its initial payload at LMA; writable runtime objects live in RAM at VMA and must be copied.
Flash stores the initial bytes without making the runtime object read-only.

question: Who creates _sdata and _ebss, and how should C use them?
options: C reads _sdata to obtain the starting address
The compiler creates initialized variables containing the boundaries
The linker defines boundaries; C takes their addresses with &
explanations: Reading _sdata reads data located there; &_sdata obtains the linker-selected boundary.
These symbols represent selected addresses rather than stored pointer variables.
The linker script defines address symbols. Use&_sdata and&_ebss to retrieve boundaries; reading the symbols as objects reads memory there.

question: Why is a missing .bss clear intermittent?
options: Prior SRAM contents vary; simulator zeros may hide missing initialization
The linker randomly relocates .bss at every reset
C automatically zeroes .bss on first read
explanations: RAM contents depend on startup/reset history; globals do not receive guaranteed zero values. Simulator or cold-boot zeros can hide the bug.
Placement is fixed in the firmware; varying contents cause the symptom.
C promises zero initialization, but startup must establish it before main.

question: Which linker map values come from the exact part datasheet, and what if RAM length is too large?
options: Declare extra RAM to make the chip physically grow its stack memory
Use the part’s actual origins/capacities; excess declared RAM can place data outside hardware
Use the 4 GB address-space size as RAM length
explanations: A linker declaration cannot create hardware; it can only hide an overflow check.
FLASH/RAM origins and lengths. A falsely large length can permit placement or a stack outside physical RAM, even if linking succeeds.
Most addressable locations are not implemented SRAM.

question: What does :020000040800 establish, and why might an 8-bit target not need it?
options: Every 8-bit processor must ignore type 04 records
It changes the CPU word size from 8 to 32 bits
Type 04 supplies high address bits; small images within 16 bits may not need it
explanations: Need depends on image addresses, not simply the processor’s data width.
HEX address records do not change the CPU’s instruction or word width.
An Intel HEX extended-linear-address record sets upper16 address bits to 0800. A small flash image within16-bit addressing needs no such upper portion.

question: Describe build-time, load-time and runtime address binding.
options: This MCU uses runtime virtual translation for each load
Build fixes firmware addresses; loading chooses a base; MMU runtime maps virtual addresses
All three mean copying .data from Flash into SRAM
explanations: This part has no MMU and uses fixed addresses selected during build.

Build-time firmware fixes addresses permanently; a loader can pick a base at start; MMU-backed runtime translation maps virtual addresses during execution. This MCU uses build time, desktops use virtual translation.
Startup copying uses chosen addresses; it does not describe all address-binding strategies.

question: Why does .bss364 bytes have no flash payload while .data96 bytes does?
options: Zeroing recreates .bss; .data needs stored initial bytes
.data takes only its size in Flash because SRAM is optional
.bss is free and consumes no SRAM
explanations: All-zero initialization can be recreated by a clear loop. Nonzero .data initial values must be stored somewhere persistent and copied.
Writable initialized objects need their SRAM run allocation as well.
It consumes runtime SRAM even without a Flash payload.

question: Compare PC and MCU bootstrap handoffs.
options: The MCU requires a desktop kernel before it can execute startup
PC firmware loads further boot stages; MCU vectors select SP/PC, then startup calls main
Both begin directly at the C main symbol without initialization
explanations: Bare-metal MCU startup runs without a kernel or process loader.
PC reset firmware loads a bootloader, then a kernel, then a user program. MCU reset loadsSP/PC from two vector words, then startup prepares C and calls main; it has no loader/OS chain.
The MCU needs hardware vector reads and startup; a PC also has earlier firmware stages.

question: Why does an ISR not require AVR’s ISR macro here?
options: Cortex-M has no saved interrupt context because only one core exists
Hardware saves the basic frame and the compiler preserves any extra callee-saved registers
An ordinary C handler never changes registers
explanations: One core still interrupts another execution sequence and must restore its context.
Hardware saves/restores the caller-clobbered frame and the C compiler preserves any callee-saved registers it uses; the vector points to an ordinary C function.
C handlers use registers; hardware and compiler preserve the required context.

question: Does volatile counter++ prevent a lost update?
options: Yes; aligned storage makes the whole increment atomic
No; volatile preserves accesses but the load/add/store can interleave
Yes; volatile makes every C expression a single instruction
explanations: Alignment can make each word access indivisible, not the complete read-modify-write sequence.
No. It forces the load/store but allows an ISR between them. Protect the whole update or give the counter one writer.
An increment still spans separate instructions.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model
question: Why can a long low-priority handler still cause trouble?
options: Low priority means it never consumes execution time
Higher-priority preemption automatically makes all shared data safe
It delays equal/lower-priority requests and can still share data with urgent handlers
explanations: It runs when selected and occupies the core until return or preemption.
Preemption enables more interleavings; it does not supply synchronization.
It blocks equal/lower-priority handlers and delays their deadlines. Shared state can also be preempted by higher-priority handlers, so duration and synchronization both matter.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model
question: Name the three hardware rendezvous methods and a suitable polling case.
options: Polling, interrupts and DMA; poll for a very short wait or acceptable human-speed sampling
DMA is always simplest even for a single rare button sample
Polling, cache and virtual memory; poll for every sustained byte stream
explanations: Polling,interrupts,DMA. Poll for a very short wait whose interrupt setup/entry overhead exceeds the wait, or a simple human-speed input where occasional sampling delay is acceptable.
DMA has configuration/ownership costs; a simple short poll can be appropriate.
Cache/virtual memory are not these notification/transfer methods; long polling can waste CPU.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model
question: Why can an interrupt handler be an ordinary C function?
options: The saved hardware frame, C ABI and vector entry cooperate with EXC_RETURN
Every ISR must manually push PC and xPSR in C
The compiler discovers handler names at runtime
explanations: Hardware savesR0–R3,R12,LR,PC,xPSR; the ABI/compiler handles any callee-saved registers it uses. The vector supplies its entry and EXC_RETURN restores the frame.
Hardware performs that basic exception-frame save before entering the handler.
Names are resolved into vector addresses during build, not searched during events.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model
question: What does volatile guarantee here, and what does it not provide?
options: Required accesses remain visible; mutual exclusion is not provided
volatile prevents all interrupts during an access sequence
volatile makes a multiword struct snapshot consistent
explanations: Required object accesses remain observable to the compiler. It supplies no mutual exclusion and cannot turn a multi-instruction increment into an atomic update.
It does not change PRIMASK or stop interrupt entry.
Separate fields can still come from different update generations.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model
question: Does a byte written only by ISR and read only by main need a critical section?

Yes; every byte access tears into multiple bus transactions
Ordinarily no for this one-writer byte access; volatile is still needed

A single aligned byte access is indivisible on this core.
Its single aligned access is indivisible and has one writer, so ordinarily no. volatile is still required; a larger related-state protocol may need protection.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model

Record minimal state and return so other work can meet deadlines
A short ISR automatically eliminates every shared-data race
explanations: Long ISR processing delays main and equal/lower-priority handlers.
They delay equal/lower-priority requests and main; long work increases latency and deadline failures. Record minimal state and process it later.
Duration reduction does not replace a correct sharing protocol.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model

Inspect races requiring rare unlucky interleavings
A long successful run proves all shared updates are atomic
explanations: Compiler visibility and interleaving bugs can both produce delayed symptoms.
A race can require a tiny unlucky interleaving. Inspect all shared variables and their operations; repeated successful runs cannot demonstrate absence of the race.
Rare windows can remain unhit for hours.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model
question: State the as-if rule and explain the hardware observer problem.

Optimization must preserve one machine instruction per C operator
The compiler knows every hardware register change without volatile
explanations: Optimization may change instructions if C-defined observable behavior is preserved. Device/ISR changes outside ordinary flow require volatile accesses so that caching/removal does not erase required observations.
The as-if rule permits a different instruction sequence with the same required behavior.
Asynchronous changes are not inferred from ordinary sequential C flow.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model
question: Define race, critical section, mutual exclusion and atomic operation generally.
options: A critical section is any function declared volatile
Race depends on ordering; protect a critical section with exclusion; atomic operations appear indivisible
Atomic means fast; mutual exclusion means low priority
explanations: volatile qualifies object accesses; it does not mark protected functions or regions.

Race: result depends on interleaving. Critical section: code that must be protected. Mutual exclusion: only one context accesses that protected region at a time. Atomic: others cannot observe the operation partly completed.
Speed and priority do not define indivisibility or exclusive access.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model
question: Why is disabling local interrupts insufficient on a dual-core processor?

Another core continues; inter-core synchronization is required
Caches always make multi-core read-modify-write updates atomic
explanations: A local interrupt mask controls that core’s configurable exceptions.
The other core continues executing. Inter-core atomic operations and synchronization are needed; a mutex can be built on them.
Cache coherence alone does not turn a multi-instruction update into one atomic operation.

topicTitle: Priority and applying the complete model
question: What is tearing, and which shared objects exhibit it here?

Tearing means a pin changes while an LED is on
A reader combines old and new parts; uint64_t and structs can exhibit it
explanations: This is a 32-bit core; a single aligned word access is indivisible here.
It concerns inconsistent shared values, not physical pin damage.
A read combines old/new components into a nonexistent logical value. A64-bit value on a 32-bit core and a multi-field structure are the two examples.

question: Why does a 4GB address space not imply4GB RAM?

The 4 GB range is Flash because the program starts there
Every 32-bit address refers to one installed SRAM byte
explanations: Addresses are names. Only mapped physical blocks respond; this part implements12 KB SRAM and 32 KB flash, with peripherals elsewhere.
The map includes many regions and holes; Flash occupies only its actual capacity.
Address width does not install memory behind every possible address.

topicTitle: RCC register map and clock gates

topicTitle: GPIO and USART maps used by startup

Output mode gives GPIO ownership; alternate mode is needed for USART ownership.
The alternate-function number does not change the pin’s analog mode.

question: Why can NMI and HardFault vectors contain the same address?

An identical target proves both source functions were strongly defined
The processor cannot distinguish NMI from HardFault
explanations: Both can be weak aliases of Default_Handler until separate strong handlers override them.
A shared weak default explains the same target without separate definitions.
They have distinct exception identities even if the default target is shared.

topicTitle: Constructing C memory and budgeting it
question: What does >RAM AT>FLASH express?
options: Runtime placement in RAM, initial load bytes in Flash
Two independent writable copies automatically synchronized forever
Execution in Flash with initial bytes stored in SRAM
explanations: The section runs in RAM but its initial bytes are stored in flash; LOADADDR supplies the source for startup copying.
Startup copies the initial bytes; later SRAM writes do not synchronize Flash.
This reverses run and load destinations.

question: Why must flash latency change before the clock?
options: Flash latency controls UART baud but not instruction fetching
Changing the clock automatically changes FLASH->ACR
Flash needs enough response time before the core runs faster
explanations: Latency concerns Flash access; UART has its own clock/divisor.
Firmware must configure the wait states in the safe order.
The faster core can otherwise fetch from flash before flash has supplied valid instruction data; the failure can appear far from clock setup.

topicTitle: Observe startup and deliberately break it
question: Why can moving the vector section create a clean build that will not boot?

Reset still reads the first Flash words as SP and target
The linker automatically teaches reset hardware the new table address
explanations: Checksums establish record integrity, not semantic correctness of startup vectors.
The linker can legally place it elsewhere, but reset hardware still reads the first two flash words as SP/PC. Those words are then code bytes rather than valid startup values.
A legal section placement does not change this hardware reset mapping.

topicTitle: Observe startup and deliberately break it
question: Predict the effect of removing the .data copy loop.

It reliably becomes zero on every device and reset
The witness in SRAM loses its guaranteed initialized value
explanations: Removing startup copying does not change Flash into runtime writable storage.
Without the copy, actual SRAM contents determine it; zero is not guaranteed.
The initialized witness is no longer guaranteed 0x00C0FFEE because its flash master is not transferred to SRAM. Record the actual replacement value in your environment.

topicTitle: Observe startup and deliberately break it
question: Predict the effect of removing the .bss clear loop.

Only Flash constants change; counters remain guaranteed zero
The compiler inserts a clear at each variable’s first use
explanations: Frame counters/zero globals begin from whatever SRAM contains. Compare runs and reset types; a simulator that initializes RAM to zero can hide the fault.
.bss is SRAM for zero-initialized globals, including counters.
Startup must zero .bss before main; there is no required first-use clear.

topicTitle: Observe startup and deliberately break it

The compiler rejects every table placed after .text
explanations: Compiler/linker/checksum validation need not enforce the reset contract. Hardware reads instruction bytes atflash base asSP/reset target rather than finding the moved table.
Section names are build metadata; reset hardware reads known addresses.
The placement can be legal to the tools while violating the reset contract.

topicTitle: Observe startup and deliberately break it

Physical SRAM shrinks to match each linker declaration

explanations: AFR[0] covers pins 0–7; pin 13 belongs to AFR[1].
AFR[1], bits 23:20: index13/8=1 and nibble shift4×(13 mod8)=20.

topicTitle: Clear a field, insert its value, then read it back

A polling read clears every edge before EXTI sees it

topicTitle: Record edges promptly and debounce in main

Writing zero to every bit clears all EXTI flags

topicTitle: Measure edges and isolate silent failures

A correctly written handler must increment unconditionally on entry

topicTitle: Priorities, cross-checks and timer lab failures

Hardware generates PWM edges; service urgency follows the deadline and overwrite risk.

Flash retains the program without power; SRAM holds temporary changing values
SRAM retains the program while Flash loses data on shutdown

All writes become RAM variables until an ISR copies them to GPIO
The CPU recognizes LED values by the number alone
explanations: A number has no intrinsic LED meaning: the destination address and register rules determine whether it is stored or drives hardware.
A direct write to a mapped GPIO command register already reaches hardware.

Clock, output mode and board wiring must all connect the command to the LED
An odd function pointer is enough to power the LED

The Thumb tag concerns code branches, not pin clocks or wiring.

CMP writes the result into the first operand
CMP sets subtraction flags without saving the subtraction result

A literal pool is a heap allocated by malloc
Every literal load transfers data from a USART receive buffer
explanations: A literal pool holds a constant the instruction cannot directly encode; a PC-relative load fetches it.
It is linked code-adjacent storage, not dynamically allocated SRAM.
Literal loads fetch constants, not inherently device payload.

Bit 0 marks Thumb state while the actual instruction address is aligned
The function begins at an unaligned odd byte in memory
explanations: An odd pointer does not represent padding or a one-byte offset.

The instruction address remains aligned; the pointer encoding includes a tag.

question: Why can compilation succeed and linking fail?
options: Compilation always links every external declaration immediately
Link failures always indicate C syntax errors
Declarations permit compilation, but linking still needs compatible definitions and valid placement
explanations: A compiler can accept an external declaration without seeing its definition.
Syntax is checked earlier; symbol resolution and memory placement are linker responsibilities.
The linker joins objects and resolves symbols; missing/duplicate definitions or region overflow can fail after each file compiled.

question: How do ELF and BIN differ?
options: BIN has more symbol/debug information than ELF
ELF is C source that a simulator must compile
ELF has sections/addresses/symbols; BIN is raw bytes needing an external base
explanations: BIN is raw data and does not contain ELF symbol/section metadata.
ELF is already-built machine code and metadata; the simulator loads it.
ELF preserves structured image and debugging information. BIN strips that structure, so its programming base must be supplied separately; HEX carries addressed records.

question: Which tools answer “what instruction?”, “what symbol address?” and “how much memory?”
options: objdump for instructions, nm for symbol addresses, size/map for memory
Use source line count for all three
nm executes the program and measures interrupt latency
explanations: Disassembly shows encoded operations; the symbol listing associates names with addresses; section sizes and the map expose memory allocation.
Source lines neither determine machine instruction encoding nor reveal linked symbol addresses or exact bytes.

question: Is an aligned 32-bit load enough to read a coherent pair of 32-bit values?
options: No; two indivisible word reads can still belong to different updates
Yes; alignment makes every adjacent pair a single atomic read
volatile forces both fields to update simultaneously
explanations: A coherent pair requires a snapshot protocol or short critical section. Atomic individual loads prevent tearing within each word, not between generations.
Two loads remain separate operations even when each address is aligned.
volatile preserves accesses without combining separate updates into one operation.

question: What is the difference between pending and active?
options: Pending means running; active means waiting
Pending is waiting for service; active is executing or suspended by a more urgent handler
Disabling an IRQ necessarily removes its pending request
explanations: This reverses the exception-state meanings.
Pending records an outstanding request. Active describes a handler whose execution has started and not yet completed; enable/masks decide when pending can start.
Enable and pending state are separate; disabling delivery can leave a recorded request waiting.

question: Why does interrupt priority affect latency?
options: More urgent eligible interrupts can preempt less urgent work; lower numbers mean higher urgency
Priority guarantees zero latency regardless of interrupt masking
Higher numeric values are always serviced first
explanations: Priority determines preemption and waiting, so it affects event-to-handler latency. Only implemented priority bits count.
Masking and even more urgent work can still delay an interrupt.
This core uses smaller numeric priority values for higher urgency.

question: Why can omitted .bss initialization seem to work in a simulator?

A simulator automatically repairs every missing startup loop
.bss is in Flash so its contents cannot vary
explanations: Startup must establish C zero initialization independent of initial RAM contents. Simulator zeros are not proof the code cleared .bss.
It may incidentally start RAM at zero; that does not repair the program’s startup contract.
.bss allocates SRAM for zero-initialized runtime objects.

question: What are .data’s two addresses?
options: Flash load address and SRAM run address
Two SRAM addresses so a background task can mirror writes
The CPU PC and LR values at reset
explanations: The load address locates persistent initial bytes; startup copies them to the run address used for writable data.
The initial image is in Flash; there is no automatic background mirroring task.
Those are control-flow state, not .data load and run locations.

question: Why might a correctly built interrupt handler never run?
options: All correctly compiled functions are registered as handlers automatically
A misspelled handler may leave the expected weak default in the vector
The debugger must call the handler once before hardware can use it
explanations: Compilation alone does not select the vector slot or replace its expected symbol.
Exact symbol names connect the vector to a strong handler definition. A different spelling can compile as an unrelated unused function.
A correct vector target works without debugger registration or an initial manual call.

question: Why is a pulled-up button active low?
options: Active low means the handler runs at lower interrupt priority
A pull-up holds released high; pressing connects ground and reads low
A pull-up actively drives zero when no button is pressed
explanations: Active-low describes signal meaning; it is unrelated to NVIC urgency.
The open switch leaves the resistor holding one. Closing the ground switch produces zero and a falling edge, so the logical pressed state is low.

question: What does FPR1=2 with NVIC IRQ 5 disabled tell you?
options: FPR1=2 means the handler has run twice
Line 1 detected a falling edge, but IRQ 5 delivery is disabled
The button edge was not detected because no handler ran
explanations: It is a bit mask identifying pending line 1, not an event counter.
FPR1 bit 1 is source evidence. Disabled NVIC IRQ 5 prevents its handler from starting, so detection can succeed while main continues.
The pending peripheral flag itself proves detection even with delivery closed.

question: Why assign a mask to an EXTI write-one-to-clear register instead of OR-ing it?
options: OR preserves all other pending flags because their values stay one
Assign only the intended mask so unrelated pending ones are not acknowledged
Assign zero to the whole register to clear the selected line
explanations: A written one clears a pending flag here, so preserving that one in the write discards its event.
A read-modify-write copies other set flags into its written value; write-one-to-clear semantics would then clear them too.
Zero leaves write-one-to-clear flags alone; the selected bit must be written as one.

question: From 0xFFFFFFF0 to 0x10, what is the elapsed unsigned 32-bit time?
options: The counter moved backwards so elapsed time is invalid
The result proves no more than 32 ticks passed regardless of observation gap
32 ticks (0x20), assuming the actual interval fits the 32-bit range
explanations: This is the normal forward wrap of an unsigned counter.
An unseen full wrap would give the same difference; a bound on the true interval is required.
Unsigned modular subtraction gives (0x10−0xFFFFFFF0) mod 2^32 = 0x20. It cannot count unseen full cycles of the counter.

question: Rise-handler delay is 10 μs and fall-handler delay is 100 μs. What error does live-CNT subtraction add?

Hardware capture inherits exactly the same +90 μs timestamp error
The delays cancel because both edges generate interrupts
explanations: Reading live CNT timestamps handler arrival. The falling handler adds 100 μs and the rising handler adds 10 μs, leaving a +90 μs error.

question: How do TIM SR and EXTI pending flags differ when clearing?
options: Both clear by reading IDR before returning
Both clear by writing one because they are status registers
Timer SR flags clear with zero; EXTI RPR1/FPR1 clear with one
explanations: GPIO input reads do not replace the documented timer/EXTI flag-clear operation.
Status register roles do not imply one universal clear convention.
Use each register’s specified convention: the relevant timer status flags are write-zero-to-clear, while EXTI pending flags are write-one-to-clear.
